title: Clean Car Discount rebates begin
summary: A rebate was paid on application to the first registered person of an eligible low-emission vehicle.

title: Clean Car Discount becomes a full feebate
summary: Rebates and fees were set by a vehicle's CO2 emissions; low-emission vehicles earned a rebate and high-emission vehicles incurred a fee.
notes: Observed at the 2026-08 snapshot (vehicles still registered): March 2022 first registrations were 43,217 against 22,195 in February and 15,553 in April; March in other years runs 18,698-24,808 (2020 excepted). Every region rose. Used petrol (7,078 to 18,853) and NZ-new diesel (5,255 to 10,543) led the rise, while NZ-new petrol hybrids (988, 482, 2,089) and plug-in hybrids (377, 437, 1,094) dipped in March and rose in April. A pull-forward case for validating the payback method; this row has neither expected_effect = pull_forward nor an announced_date yet.

title: Clean Car Discount settings changed
summary: Policy changes to the Clean Car Discount took effect from July 2023.
notes: Observed at the 2026-08 snapshot (vehicles still registered): June 2023 first registrations were 39,479 against 22,401 in May and 12,282 in July; June in 2015-2025 otherwise runs 16,942-24,827. Every region and every major powertrain rose, NZ-new (12,949 to 22,902) and used (9,452 to 16,577) alike. A second pull-forward case, independent of clean-car-discount-repeal, for validating the payback method; this row has neither expected_effect = pull_forward nor an announced_date yet.

title: Clean Car Discount ends
summary: Charges and rebates ended for vehicles registered after 11.59pm on 31 December 2023. The repeal Act passed all three readings under urgency on 14 December 2023 and received royal assent on 19 December.

title: Clean Car fees no longer apply
summary: From 1 January 2024 no vehicle was subject to a Clean Car Discount fee. Expect a mirror-image effect: high-emission registrations deferred into January.

title: Clean Car Standard applies to importers
summary: A CO2 standard applying to vehicle importers rather than buyers. It survived the repeal of the Clean Car Discount and continues to shape what importers choose to bring in.

title: Clean Car Standard targets weakened to align with Australia
summary: Annual CO2 targets for 2025-2029 were reset. Commercial vehicle targets start at 223 g/km in 2025 falling to 131 g/km by 2029. Credit lifespan extended from three to four years and credit transfer between new and used sectors permitted from 2026.

title: Clean Car Standard charges cut by around 80 percent
summary: The top rate for new vehicles fell from $67.50 to $15 per gram of CO2 and for used vehicles from $33.75 to $7.50. Existing credits protected from expiring before 31 December 2028. At the time 86 percent of importers faced a net charge.

title: Clean Car Standard retained after review
summary: The Government kept the Standard rather than scrapping it and will introduce separate targets for used imports. New settings take effect 1 January 2028 with officials reporting back early 2027. Current targets are 108 g/km for 2026 falling to 103 g/km in 2027.

title: Road user charges applied to light EVs and PHEVs
summary: Light electric vehicles and plug-in hybrids became subject to RUC ending the previous exemption. BEVs pay a full rate and PHEVs a reduced rate.

title: Heavy electric vehicles begin paying RUC
summary: Electric vehicles over 3500 kg become subject to road user charges.

title: Government announces transition of all light vehicles to RUC
summary: At Building Nations 2025 the Transport Minister announced next steps to move New Zealand's 3.5 million light vehicles from fuel excise duty to electronic road user charges. Described by the Minister as the biggest change to road funding in 50 years.

title: RUC legislation expected to pass
summary: The Minister expects the enabling legislation to pass during 2026. No date has been set for the full transition of the light fleet.

title: RUC system open to third-party providers
summary: By 2027 the RUC system is intended to be open for business with third-party providers offering payment services, electronic licences and post-pay billing.

title: Planned 12 cents per litre fuel excise increase scrapped
summary: The Government scrapped a fuel excise increase planned for 2027 and delayed the next road user charge rise by a year.

title: Fuel excise duty cut by 25 cents a litre
summary: A temporary cut in response to fuel prices after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, extended three times before ending 30 June 2023. Petrol excise fell from 70.024 to 45.02 cents per litre.

title: Road user charges cut 36 percent
summary: A temporary 36 percent reduction across all RUC rates as part of the cost-of-living package.

title: Road user charges cut 36 percent again
summary: The RUC reduction was reinstated for a second window before standard rates resumed on 1 July 2023.

title: Auckland regional fuel tax introduced
summary: An additional 11.5 cents per litre on petrol and diesel applying only in the Auckland region.

title: Auckland regional fuel tax abolished
summary: The 11.5 cents per litre regional tax ended, removing an Auckland-only fuel cost that had run for six years.

title: Time of use charging law comes into force
summary: The Land Transport Management (Time of Use Charging) Amendment Act 2025 received royal assent on 18 November 2025 and comes into force 18 November 2026. Passed unanimously by all six parties.

title: Auckland congestion charging consultation opens
summary: Auckland Council narrowed proposals to three options with charges from $2 to $7 covering the city centre, a wider central cordon and central motorways. Final decision expected 2028 with introduction possible from 2030 or 2031.

title: General election
summary: The Prime Minister announced on 21 January 2026 that the general election will be held on Saturday 7 November 2026. The 2023 change of government moved on vehicle policy within weeks of taking office.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12. The Beehive release title gives the date; interest.co.nz (21 January 2026) reports the announcement at the National Party caucus retreat in Christchurch. The seeded summary said a change of government had twice reset vehicle policy within weeks and advised treating the following six months as elevated policy risk; neither was sourced, so the summary keeps only the date and the 2023 precedent (coalition-government-2023).

title: Change of government
summary: A National-ACT-NZ First coalition took office and moved on vehicle policy within its first weeks, repealing the Clean Car Discount and committing to end the Auckland regional fuel tax.

title: Electronic stability control required on all new light vehicles
summary: ESC became mandatory for all newly registered new light passenger and goods vehicles.

title: ESC required on used SUV and off-road imports
summary: Class MC vehicles entering New Zealand from 1 March 2016 had to have ESC fitted and working at border inspection, removing a slice of used import supply.

title: ESC required on used passenger cars over 2 litres
summary: Used class MA passenger cars with engine capacity above 2 litres inspected at the border from 1 March 2018 had to have ESC fitted.
notes: Date corrected 2026-09-12 from 2018-01-01. NZTA's entry certification notice and IMVIA's advice (Autofile, 8 January 2016) both give 1 March 2018; the earlier Stuff source did not.

title: ESC required on all remaining used light imports
summary: The final stage of the ESC phase-in: all other used class MA, MB and NA light passenger and goods vehicles inspected at the border from 1 March 2020 had to have ESC fitted.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12. NZTA's notice for the 1 March 2018 stage names 1 March 2020 for the final stage, and IMVIA's advice (Autofile, 8 January 2016, https://autofile.co.nz/imvia-advice-on-esc-rule-) gives the same three dates: 1 March 2016, 2018 and 2020. The seeded summary's alternative of 1 January 2020 has no source. Vintage, motorsport and scratch-built vehicles are exempt.

title: Japanese emissions code requirements tightened
summary: For vehicles border-inspected from 30 April 2024 the required standard depends on the emissions-code prefix on the Japanese export certificate. Industry sources report this effectively closed the import channel for many vehicles manufactured between roughly 2006 and 2012 while vehicles over 20 years old remain importable. Probably the largest structural change to used import supply in a decade.

title: Toyota New Zealand moves to an agency model
summary: The Drive Happy Project replaced dealer-owned stock and price negotiation with fixed national pricing and three distributor-held vehicle pools. Dealers became agents earning a fee. MEASUREMENT WARNING: this changes who is recorded as the registering party and how demonstrator stock enters the register.

title: Mercedes-Benz moves to an agency model
summary: Mercedes-Benz announced a shift to an agency sales model in selected markets including New Zealand. Same measurement caveat as Toyota. VERIFY EXACT NZ START DATE.
notes: Checked 2026-09-12, left unverified: no source gives the start date. Announced for January 2022 (Autotalk, 3 August 2020), postponed to the second half of 2022 (Autofile, 6 April 2022), and reported as launched on 9 August 2022 (Autofile, https://autofile.co.nz/marque-launches-agency-model-). The 2022-01-01 date_start is the original plan, which did not happen. The register shows no step in MERCEDES-BENZ first registrations during 2022 apart from the March feebate spike.

title: Holden Commodore nameplate discontinued
summary: Holden announced the end of the Commodore after 41 years to focus on SUVs and utes.

title: Holden brand retired
summary: General Motors announced on 17 February 2020 that Holden would be retired from sale in Australia and New Zealand. The marque was defunct from 1 January 2021. Holden remains a large share of the used fleet so the effect on stock and flow charts diverges sharply.

title: BYD enters New Zealand
summary: BYD Auto New Zealand, distributed by Ateco Automotive, announced on 8 June 2022 a launch in the third quarter, with the all-electric Atto 3 opening for presales in July. Customer handovers were under way by late August, while the Clean Car Discount was in force.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12. The Driven (24 August 2022) reported a customer handover in Auckland. Observed at the 2026-08 snapshot (vehicles still registered): BYD first registrations were single vehicles in 2021 and early 2022, then 20 in July 2022 and 444 in August. date_start is July, the presales month and the first month with more than two.

title: Wave of Chinese brand entries
summary: Ten of the fourteen Chinese brands present in New Zealand launched within three years. Chinese brands now outnumber Japanese and Korean brands here for the first time: BYD, Chery, Geely, GWM, JAC, Jaecoo, LDV, Leapmotor, MG and Omoda, with XPeng, IM, Zeekr and Farizon confirmed.

title: Four more Chinese brands confirmed
summary: XPeng, IM, Zeekr and Farizon confirmed New Zealand launches.

title: BYD expands New Zealand range
summary: BYD launched the Atto 1, Atto 2, Sealion 5 and Sealion 8 in early 2026, adding to the Shark 6, Sealion 6, Sealion 7, Dolphin, Seal and Atto 3.

title: BYD Atto 3 sourcing shifts to Thailand
summary: A run of Thai-built Atto 3 units replaced Chinese-built cars for New Zealand with a price drop. A clean worked example of brand origin and country of manufacture diverging within a single nameplate.

title: Fuel prices spike after Russia's invasion of Ukraine
summary: Fuel prices rose sharply worldwide. New Zealand fuel prices had already risen 13 percent by February 2022.

title: Fuel price spike drives electrified registrations
summary: Petrol and diesel prices rose sharply from late February 2026. Battery electric and plug-in hybrid passenger vehicles reached 36.7 percent combined share in July 2026 against 12.8 percent year-to-date a year earlier.

title: COVID-19 border closure
summary: New Zealand's border closed to everyone except citizens and residents on 19 March 2020 and fully reopened to all travellers and visa holders on 31 July 2022. The window marks the border settings for people; vehicle shipping and supply disruption over the period did not follow these dates.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12 against the Royal Commission of Inquiry into COVID-19 Lessons Learned. The seeded title and summary tied supply disruption to this window; no source dates supply disruption to the border settings, so the title now names only the border closure. Open question: category and mechanism are still supply, though the border restricted people rather than vehicles.

title: First national COVID-19 lockdown
summary: New Zealand moved to Alert Level 4 on 25 March 2020 and to Alert Level 3 on 27 April, and lifted the remaining lockdown restrictions with the move to Alert Level 2 on 13 May. April 2020 is a near-zero month for first registrations, which distorts year-on-year comparisons through 2021.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12. Observed at the 2026-08 snapshot (vehicles still registered): in-scope first registrations were 22,626 in January 2020, 15,345 in March, 1,542 in April, 16,292 in May and 21,563 in June. The seeded summary expected a catch-up spike after the lockdown; no month rises above January, so that claim was removed.

title: Extended Auckland COVID-19 lockdown
summary: New Zealand moved to Alert Level 4 on 17 August 2021. The rest of the country was at Alert Level 2 by 7 September, while Auckland stayed at Alert Level 3 or higher until 2 December, when the traffic light system replaced alert levels. Creates a regional divergence visible in registrations by region.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12. Observed at the 2026-08 snapshot (vehicles still registered): Auckland's share of in-scope first registrations was 35.8% in July 2021, 36.9% in August (nationwide lockdown), 26.8% in September and 35.7% in October, so the divergence is concentrated in September.

title: Global semiconductor shortage
summary: Chip supply constraints limited new vehicle availability and lengthened delivery times. Registrations in this period reflect supply not demand.
notes: Checked 2026-09-12, left unverified: no source dates a start or an end for New Zealand, so the 2021-01-01 to 2022-12-31 window is a convention. RNZ (21 May 2021, https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/business/443046/new-car-availability-hits-low-point-due-to-computer-chip-shortages) quotes the Motor Industry Association: distributor stock at about a quarter of the normal three to four months' supply, with no end in sight.

title: Reserve Bank tightening cycle, 2021-2023
summary: The Reserve Bank raised the official cash rate from 0.25 percent to 5.5 percent between 6 October 2021 and 24 May 2023.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12 against RBNZ decision releases: OCR raised to 0.5% on 6 October 2021 (the first increase) and to 5.5% on 24 May 2023 (the last). The window runs from the first increase to the last; the OCR then held at 5.5% until 14 August 2024. A second tightening cycle began in July 2026 (OCR raised to 2.5%, then 2.75% in September) and has no row yet.

title: Reserve Bank easing cycle, 2024-2025
summary: The Reserve Bank cut the official cash rate from 5.5 percent to 2.25 percent between 14 August 2024 and 26 November 2025.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12 against RBNZ decision releases: OCR cut to 5.25% on 14 August 2024 (the first cut) and to 2.25% on 26 November 2025 (the last). The window runs from the first cut to the last; the OCR held at 2.25% until it was raised in July 2026.

title: Weak yen lowers used import cost
summary: A weaker yen reduces the landed cost of Japanese used imports and typically lifts volumes. Consider modelling as a continuous series rather than a discrete event.
notes: Checked 2026-09-12, left unverified: a currency level has no start or end date for a source to confirm. Better published as a continuous exchange-rate series than as an event, as the summary says.

title: Honda New Zealand agency model
summary: Honda operated an agency system in New Zealand before Toyota's 2018 move. VERIFY START DATE. Same measurement caveat.
notes: Checked 2026-09-12, left unverified: GoAuto (10 March 2020, https://premium.goauto.com.au/honda-poised-to-move-to-agency-model/) says Honda New Zealand first introduced the agency model in 2000, but no source found gives a month, and the register shows no step in HONDA first registrations during 2000 (84-177 a month still registered). Honda reorganised its agents into three store types from May 2021 (Autofile, 9 March 2021).

title: Tesla establishes New Zealand presence
summary: Tesla announced its official New Zealand launch in November 2016 and handed cars to its first eight New Zealand customers at a launch event in Auckland in February 2017.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12. Teslarati (26 February 2017) reports the launch event on the Thursday evening before; Electrek reported the official New Zealand launch on 21 November 2016. One search summary gave May 2017; no page found supports it. date_start is the first of the month because registrations can precede the event. Observed at the 2026-08 snapshot (vehicles still registered): TESLA first registrations run at 0-6 a month from August 2012, then 16 in February 2017 and 19 in March.

title: MG relaunched under SAIC ownership
summary: SAIC Motor took over distribution of MG in New Zealand, announced in February 2019, and the first dealerships opened in April 2019 selling the MG3 and the MG ZS.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12. Driven (20 February 2019) reports SAIC taking over distribution with the MG3 and MG ZS arriving once dealerships were set up; Driven (2 May 2019) reports the Auckland dealership as MG's fourth, after Tauranga, Palmerston North and Christchurch. The April 2019 opening month rests on trade press summaries and the register: MG first registrations were 0-6 a month through March 2019, then 33 in April, 46 in May and 102 in October. Earlier MG registrations are older vehicles from previous owners of the marque.

title: SsangYong renamed KG Mobility
summary: SsangYong New Zealand became KGM at the end of March 2024, a renaming after the company's acquisition by KG Group, not a market entry. The brand registry maps SSANGYONG and KG MOBILITY to KGM, so the make series is continuous.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12. Auto Trader, Driven and Inchcape (all 7 March 2024) say the transition happens at the end of March, with dealer signage changing over the following months. No source gives a day, so date_start is the last day of March.

title: Takata airbag recall
summary: A compulsory recall of Takata Alpha airbag inflators, announced on 4 April 2018, took effect on 31 May 2018: affected vehicles became prohibited imports and could not be sold in trade until remedied, and entry certifiers rejected vehicles flagged with an open airbag recall until the airbags were shown to be replaced. Non-Alpha Takata recalls were flagged at the border from 1 November 2018.
notes: Verified 2026-09-12 against NZTA's entry certification technical bulletin and Product Safety NZ. The seeded summary mentioned deregistrations; no source found supports that, so it was removed. Recall repairs were due by 31 December 2019, but unremedied vehicles remain prohibited imports, so the row has no date_end.

title: Diesel mild hybrids enter the register
summary: Toyota New Zealand began delivering Hilux utes with a 48V mild-hybrid system on the 2.8-litre diesel in early 2024, and the register records them as diesel hybrids: a change in what the manufacturer fitted, not in what buyers chose.
